title: White and Black players and the beat; Doc Evans's advice
summary: DeVore says white players land on the beat and Black players play against it, recalling Doc Evans telling him to play off the beat; Allen compares clapping on one and three.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: That is, that's where most white, like, for instance, the Blue Water School, the West Coast School of traditional jazz, that all seemed to me to be something they missed. They all came down to beat at the same time. The tonality was there, I always liked Lou Waters playing. He seemed to get a hot tone, but when he, his phrasing always sounded stiff to me because they were always going plump, plump, plump right on the beat. And all the good guys, the guys that I've admired the most and to me that play the most jazz, always had the phrasing that was off the beat. And I didn't realize that myself while I was down here. That's something that never was explained to me. I didn't realize it until I was playing out of Doc Evans' place up in Mendota, Minnesota. And we were playing and Doc Evans came up to me and said, gee, why don't you play a little bit more off the beat? I think it would help. And when he said that, I realized that that was where I was having so much trouble.
you were coming down right on the beat.

Right on the beat. I don't know if it's a natural thing for white musicians or not. Color musicians seem to instinctively play against the beat. Before or after all. Yeah. White musicians instinctively seem to hit at the same time. Well, you yourself can tell if you watch the people over that preservation hall. They're all stomping the foot. They understand that. And when they clap, they clap on the beat. One and three. Maybe a musician wouldn't, but the majority of the people, whenever you hear people clapping if they're white, they're on one and three almost invariably. And that's another form of being on the beat, so to speak.
Well, I notice that when I'm with a crowd of white people that I tend to clap on one and three, you know.
They do. But if I'm with colored people, you know, say at a parade, well, then I feel the two and four much more. You know, I'm more relaxed around them or something
and it comes more easily to me. Yeah, well, these are all things that a band has to keep in mind and it's a job
